title: Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories

paper.title: Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories
paper.abstract:
Abstract AI agent performance is not just a modeling problem, it is fundamentally a
systems problem. The advanced capabilities of models are realized through agent harnesses.
Therefore, a gap between model assumptions and harness behavior can easily prevent the model’s full capabilities from translating into agent performance.
We formalize this as the ‘intent-execution’ gap: the mismatch between
what the model intends and what the harness executes, and vice versa.
We argue that minimizing this intent-execution gap is as important as other aspects of harness design such as tools and execution loops.
To illustrate the impact of this harness-model alignment, we develop a simple and customizable harness called ‘Simple Strands Agent’ (SSA). SSA aims to find the bulk of common patterns which generalize across different model families (such as Claude, Gemini, GPT, Grok, Qwen), as well as a small number of model-specific preferences.
We make two contributions: (i) we reproduce or improve on the pass@1 performance reported by diverse model-provider families on popular agentic benchmarks (SWE-Pro, SWE-Verified, Terminal-Bench-2, and Deep-SWE), and (ii) building on an analysis of 154 k trajectories generated by SSA , we look beyond the pass@1 numbers which tend to be relatively even across frontier models.
By representing agent trajectories in code state-spaces, we compute solution distance and backtracking to observe model-level differences in problem-solving behavior.
Finer-grained metrics such as edit frequency, testing activity, and phase-transitions reveal how individual models allocate effort across different stages of problem solving. Code: https://github.com/strands-labs/benchmark-harnesses

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2606.17454v3 [cs.AI] 01 Oct 2026 Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories Gaurav Gupta Vatshank Chaturvedi Sudipta Sengupta Jun Huan & Anoop Deoras Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Affiliation: {gauravaz, vatshc, sudipta, lukehuan, adeoras}@amazon.com Abstract AI agent performance is not just a modeling problem, it is fundamentally a systems problem. The advanced capabilities of models are realized through agent harnesses. Therefore, a gap between model assumptions and harness behavior can easily prevent the model’s full capabilities from translating into agent performance. We formalize this as the ‘intent-execution’ gap: the mismatch between what the model intends and what the harness executes, and vice versa. We argue that minimizing this intent-execution gap is as important as other aspects of harness design such as tools and execution loops. To illustrate the impact of this harness-model alignment, we develop a simple and customizable harness called ‘Simple Strands Agent’ (SSA). SSA aims to find the bulk of common patterns which generalize across different model families (such as Claude, Gemini, GPT, Grok, Qwen), as well as a small number of model-specific preferences. We make two contributions: (i) we reproduce or improve on the pass@1 performance reported by diverse model-provider families on popular agentic benchmarks (SWE-Pro, SWE-Verified, Terminal-Bench-2, and Deep-SWE), and (ii) building on an analysis of 154 k trajectories generated by SSA , we look beyond the pass@1 numbers which tend to be relatively even across frontier models. By representing agent trajectories in code state-spaces, we compute solution distance and backtracking to observe model-level differences in problem-solving behavior. Finer-grained metrics such as edit frequency, testing activity, and phase-transitions reveal how individual models allocate effort across different stages of problem solving. Code: https://github.com/strands-labs/benchmark-harnesses 1 Introduction A modern coding agent couples an LLM with a harness , the software layer that mediates every tool call, feeds execution outcomes back into the context window, and manages the thought-action-observation loop ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Xi et al., 2023 ; Schluntz and Zhang, 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . As base models improve, the alignment of the model with the harness becomes critical to realizing the model’s full capabilities. Informally, given two models ℳ A > ℳ B \mathcal{M}_{A}>\mathcal{M}_{B} in raw capability, a harness H H without such alignment can yield acc ⁡ ( H , ℳ A ) ≈ acc ⁡ ( H , ℳ B ) \mathrm{acc}(H,\mathcal{M}_{A})\approx\mathrm{acc}(H,\mathcal{M}_{B}) where a ​ c ​ c acc is accuracy. We formalize this misalignment between harness and model as the intent-execution gap : a bidirectional mismatch between what the model intends and what the harness executes, and between what happened in the environment and what is revealed to the model . The gap is bidirectional because failures compound in both directions as a misinterpreted edit silently corrupts state, and an under-specified execution result leads the model to reason from false premises. For instance, a model may intend to replace a single occurrence of a function call, while the harness silently patches every match; or a long shell output may be truncated in a way that hides the test failure the model needs to see. Problem-specific tunings such as bespoke prompts ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Kojima et al., 2023 ) , specialized tool schemas ( Schick et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2023 ) , or hand-crafted execution graphs ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) can reduce this gap for a given model on a given benchmark. But such gains are brittle. As models improve ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , behaviors shift and optimizations that overfit one model’s quirks can degrade on the next ( Schluntz and Zhang, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) . This motivates a different strategy: rather than only chasing model-specific tricks, identify invariant interface principles that remain effective across model families, model generations, and benchmarks, and adapt only where families genuinely differ. This perspective raises two fundamental questions at the model-harness boundary: 1. Does the harness faithfully execute what the model intended? 2. Is the model given an accurate account of what the harness did? We show that minimizing this bidirectional gap without task-specific tuning is sufficient to match or exceed official benchmark numbers for models we evaluate across seven families (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, Kimi, Muse Spark, Qwen) on SWE-Bench-Verified, SWE-Bench-Pro, Terminal-Bench-2 and Deep-SWE. We also analyze SSA trajectories to answer a question that pass@1 cannot: how do different model families solve the same problems? By projecting agent state into a text-level code space and measuring distance to verified solutions at each cycle, we surface stable behavioral signatures (Section 3 ) in the form of tool-call intent, phase (exploration vs implementation), backtracking rates that differentiate families even when their pass@1 scores are indistinguishable. Main Contributions. 1. We introduce Simple Strands Agent (SSA), an open-source harness designed around the intent-execution gap, and show that it reproduces or exceeds the published benchmark numbers for 61 of 66 model–benchmark pairs across seven model families on SWE-Bench-Verified, SWE-Bench-Pro, Terminal-Bench-2 and Deep-SWE. 2. We define a solution-distance metric over a text-level code space that tracks, at each agent cycle, how far the repository state is from a verified-correct fix, and decompose it exactly into best-so-far progress and a backtracking term, giving backtracking a precise and time-dependent definition. 3. We present a trajectory-level analysis across all 38 evaluated models revealing family-specific behavioral signatures such as edit/test ratios, phase schedules, and backtracking patterns, that are stable across benchmarks and invisible to aggregate metrics. 4. We identify and quantify a git-history leakage channel in the public SWE-Bench-Pro containers that inflates measured pass@1 by up to 6.9 % 6.9\% for the affected models (Appendix ). Section 2 explains harness improvements that make SSA effective, Section 3 introduces a framework for tracking agent code-states as they evolve over the course of a trajectory, and Section 4 reports SSA’s performance on agentic benchmarks and the analysis of model trajectories. Appendix A outlines the SSA architecture. 2 SSA Refinements We now describe methods that make SSA effective, namely, feedback-rich tool boundaries in Section 2.1 , our approach to prompting agents for a better balance between reasoning and tool-use in Section 2.2 , as well as leaning on the model’s preferences for tool interfaces in Section 2.3 . 2.1 Feedback-rich tool boundaries The key design principle of the SSA harness is to make the information exchanged at the model-tools boundary transparent and explicit. We do so through the following mechanisms: Structured execution feedback. All shell calls return the following information: command, status, exit code, output, and error text. When interrupted by a timeout, partial output is returned when available. Long outputs are clipped in the middle but preserve the start and end of the outputs so that failure summaries and final test results are not lost. Safer editing semantics. All edits are anchored to neighboring lines. Partial-line matches and duplicate matches are rejected with feedback that helps the model disambiguate and issue a more precise edit in the next turn. Successful edits return a unified diff reducing the need for the model to verify if the intended change was actually applied. 2.2 Balancing reasoning with tool-calling Chain-of-thought reasoning ( Wei et al., 2023 ; Kojima et al., 2023 ) is clearly valuable. It allows the model to decompose a problem, plan next-steps, and decide which tool to invoke. Without sufficient reasoning, tool-usage becomes reactive, leading to shallow exploration, redundant calls, or poor sequencing of actions. However, excessive thinking introduces its own failure mode. When the model spends too long reasoning internally, it begins to form assumptions about the environment rather than verifying them. As a result, the agent may issue poorly grounded tool calls or skip necessary validation steps altogether, creating a fundamental tension between the model’s internal state and the external environment. Effective agents must continuously reconcile these two demands, and we refer to this balance as tool calling with a reasoning nudge . The idea is to encourage the model to perform just enough reasoning to decide the next action and then prioritize evidence-gathering interactions with the environment over further reasoning. Rather than extending internal chains-of-thought, the agent is nudged toward validating its hypotheses through tool outputs ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) . In practice, we did not find a single ‘‘golden prompt’’ that reliably balances reasoning and tool interaction across all model families. For the Claude variants, we found that a quantitative target, e.g., ‘‘make 50+ tool calls’’ or ‘‘ideal tool call count is 100’’ 1 1 1 This style of quantitative tool-call prompt first appeared in the Claude Sonnet 4.5 release: https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-sonnet-4-5 . helps shift the balance from reasoning toward interaction with the environment. While the exact number of target tool calls is not important, it serves as a useful north star that biases the model toward action. Under the same prompt, Gemini and Grok runs frequently emitted empty tool calls up to the stated mark. Here, we found that using a qualitative direction such as “You should use tools as much as possible” achieves the same balance. Figure 1: Reasoning nudges in SSA : Each family is nudged toward tool use in the form, quantitative or qualitative, it responds to. 2.3 Aligning harness with the model’s tool use preferences Across agents, while tools function in exactly the same way, models tend to exhibit distinct preferences in how they invoke them. For example, GPT models prefer to update code by using an apply_patch command to splice in text from a separate file, formatted in a particular way. Performance depends on honoring these formatting preferences ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Xia et al., 2024 ) . Similarly, for Grok-4.20, a single monolithic tool for editing and viewing performs poorly, whereas splitting functionality into atomic operations yields better results even though the functionality remains unchanged. Additionally, viewing line numbers in a file helps most models, but Grok has trouble separating prefixes from line numbers. Here, disabling line-numbers helps the model use the view-tool effectively. These preferences are a by-product of training, and an effective harness should leverage them rather than fight them ( Schluntz and Zhang, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) . This reinforces a broader design principle that agent performance is a function of not only what tools are available but also how naturally those tools align with the model’s learned behaviors. A well-designed harness should meet the model where it is, adapting interfaces and feedback to its strengths while still enforcing the invariants needed for reliable execution. 3 Solution distance: measuring trajectory quality Motivation. Standard agentic-coding metrics such as pass@1, tool-calls distribution, number of output-tokens summarize outcome and cost but not the trajectory quality . Two runs that achieve similar pass@1 on the same instance can still differ markedly. One may proceed through a clean explore → \to localize → \to implement → \to verify arc with a single decisive edit while another may oscillate between candidate fixes, undo and reapply edits, or commit a correct patch and subsequently retract it. To study and isolate this behavior, we introduce metrics in this subsubsection that answer a single, mechanistic question at every point in a trajectory: how close is the agent’s current repository state to a verified-correct solution for this instance, and does it move monotonically towards one or does it backtrack? Interestingly, this signal can remain positive while a run recovers from an earlier reversal. 4 Experimental Results We evaluate SSA on four agentic benchmarks, namely, SWE-Bench-Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , SWE-Bench-Pro ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , Terminal-Bench-2 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) and Deep-SWE ( DataCurve, 2026 ) and seven model families: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, Kimi, Muse Spark and Qwen. Under one harness, SSA reproduces or exceeds the published pass@1 for 61 of the 66 model–benchmark pairs with a published figure, and is ahead of widely-used open-source harnesses. Next, in this Section, we analyze trajectories ( 154 154 k in total) from all these runs to better understand how each model-family approaches problem solving, information that is not expressed just looking at pass@1. 4.1 Setup and protocol Experimental-setup details (compute cluster, model serving, per-model inference settings, and the evaluation-hygiene protocol) are given in Appendix , and the prompts in Appendix . All four benchmark ship with pre-existing tests. The SWE benchmarks serialize the agent’s workspace changes into a patch and replay it in a separate evaluator container. Terminal-Bench-2 evaluates in-place but imposes explicit per-task compute and wall-time limits that the SWE benchmarks do not. Throughout, we report pass@1 following the convention of Chen et al. (2021) . We follow a strict routine of counting every failure (agent or infra) into pass@1 and not alter denominator which otherwise can inflate the scores. Each model is run five times on the full benchmark. In total we evaluate 38 models (see Appendix ). The main sweep of 21 models over three benchmarks yields ( 500 + 731 + 89 ) × 5 × 21 = 138,600 (500+731+89)\times 5\times 21=138{,}600 trajectories; the second Terminal-Bench-2 setting for the 13 closed models adds 89 × 5 × 13 = 5,785 89\times 5\times 13=5{,}785 , and the 17 models on Deep-SWE add 113 × 5 × 17 = 9,605 113\times 5\times 17=9{,}605 yielding 153,990 153{,}990 trajectories in total, ≈ 154 \approx 154 k, which we analyze further for model behavior. 4.2 Published pass rates are recovered under one harness SSA reproduces or exceeds official model-card numbers under a single harness . Every model is run under the same execution loop, feedback semantics and evaluation protocol (Section 4.1 ); only the narrow interface adapters of Appendix differ. Tables 1 and 2 record, for each model and benchmark, whether the figure the provider publishes falls inside SSA’s 95 % 95\% confidence interval, below it, or above it. Appendix reports the mean per-run resolution rate with 95 % 95\% confidence intervals over all per-instance trials ( 2,500 2{,}500 for SWE-Bench-Verified, 3,655 3{,}655 for SWE-Bench-Pro, 445 445 for Terminal-Bench-2, and 565 565 for Deep-SWE). Of the 66 model–benchmark pairs for which a published figure exists (43 in Table 1 , 17 in Table 2 , and 6, all reproduced, from models added after the main sweep that appear only in Appendix ), 61 fall within or below SSA’s interval (44 reproduced and 17 exceeded) and 5 lie above it, four of them on SWE-Bench-Pro, whose public containers leak future git history (Appendix ; per-model figures in Appendix ). These results characterize model–harness configurations under the stated evaluation conditions and they do not establish a general ordering of provider capability. For Terminal-Bench-2 we report two settings (motivated in Appendix ): Constrained , which honors the benchmark’s memory and time budgets, and Unconstrained , which removes them and acts as an upper bound on performance. Providers report their figures under the Constrained setting, except for the Qwen models, whose published figures are Unconstrained; Table 1 compares each published figure against the matching setting. Open-source models were run only Unconstrained. Overall, we found that removing the memory and agent-time limits lifts pass@1 by roughly 5 5 - 10 % 10\% across models (see Appendix ). Taken together, the benchmark results show that a harness built to minimize the intent-execution gap, with only narrow family-level interface adapters, recovers published performance, within confidence intervals, for 61 of the 66 model-benchmark pairs, and out-performs the default open-source harnesses practitioners typically use. 4.3 Trajectory-level analysis Performance via pass@1 reports whether a run was successfully resolved but says nothing about how . Using an (i) LLM-judge (see Appendix B.1.1 for details), we label each trajectory’s tool-calls across R1-R8 rubrics as detailed in Table . We partition tool calls into source-edit, scratch-testing (tests written by the agent itself), and suite-testing labels (pre-existing tests in the repository). We calculate the per-cycle R6 phase composition ( explore / localize / implement / verify ). Next, (ii) with code state-space, the solution-distance curve D ⁡ ( t ) D(t) and backtracking signal B ⁡ ( t ) B(t) (see Appendix ) are captured. Together, these metrics give us a better understanding of how the models work in the setting of an agentic problem solving. Terminal-Bench-2 scores are sensitive to evaluation infrastructure. Beyond model quality, Terminal-Bench-2 results also reflect the stability of the serving and execution stack: inference-backend throughput, node packing, command batching, and the benchmark’s own memory and time budgets each move pass@1 by 5 5 – 10 10 points. We analyse these effects in Appendix . 5 Conclusion As frontier models grow more capable, the harness is critical in determining whether that capability is translated into agent performance or lost in the interface between model and environment. A good harness (i) applies the principles that help every model family, such as line-anchored edits, explicit post-edit diffs, and faithful tool-output serialization, and (ii) adapts to the model’s preferences where model-families genuinely differ. Our experiments show that minimizing the bidirectional intent–execution gap is enough to bring the models we test to or above their reported model card numbers, within confidence intervals, in 61 of 66 cases on SWE-Bench-Pro, SWE-Bench-Verified, Terminal-Bench-2 and Deep-SWE with no task-specific tuning; 4 of the remaining 5 are on SWE-Bench-Pro, whose public containers carry a leakage artifact (Section 4.2 ). The gap between documented and reproduced agent performance is therefore in large part harness friction rather than any fundamental limitation of a simple ReACT ( Yao et al., 2023 ) based single-agent design. And because no tool surface is uniformly best, the goal is to have a harness that holds execution invariants fixed while meeting each model-family where its training left it. We see that as models converge near the top of these benchmarks, pass@1 stops separating them but their trajectories do not. Our code state-space analysis (solution-distance, backtracking) and phase decomposition show that models with the same solve rate can differ in the path taken by their corresponding agents in code-state space. Going beyond accuracy numbers and understanding trajectory behavior is what makes model-harness co-design possible. It has the following components: tasks, prompts, models, tools, environments, and hooks. The input task is converted into prompts, with the agent alternating between model calls and tool execution. Tasks and model adapters feed a cyclic SimpleStrandAgent loop. The loop streams model output, dispatches tools, executes them in the environment, and appends tool results to conversation state. Hooks validate bounds and record the loop; termination extracts the final environment state and diff patch. Task and prompts. The task to be solved is converted to a user prompt and paired with system prompts that may include model-specific instructions (see Appendix for complete set of SSA prompts). Model specific changes may include reasoning nudge (see Section 2.2 ) and tool-specific instructions such as apply_patch for GPT family. Model interface. Adapters map model-provider APIs into a common event interface: assistant text, reasoning content, tool-use requests, stop reasons, usage, cache metadata, and recoverable errors. The event loop is the same across all models. Agent core and conversation. The core is a thin control loop: call the model, execute requested tools, append tool results, and repeat. Appendix B Methodology and Metrics All quantitative results in Section 4 are computed from two artifacts produced by every SSA evaluation. (1) A metrics.json with the per-cycle token, latency, cache and tool-success counters emitted by the harness, and (2) trajectory.json containing every user / assistant message (with reasoning blocks, tool calls and tool results) verbatim. The trajectory is the authoritative input to all behavioral analyses, whenever counters in metrics.json disagree with the trajectory (e.g. retry due to exception handling) the trajectory wins. B.1 Methodology All behavioral analyses are driven by a per-call LLM judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) that classifies every tool invocation against a fixed rubric. This subsection describes the judge pipeline, the rubric it operates on, and the system prompt under which it runs. B.1.1 LLM judge for tool-call classification Every individual tool call in the trajectory is classified against a fixed rubric by a Claude Opus 4.6 judge ( Anthropic, 2025 ) . The pipeline works as follows: 1. Windowed classification. Each trajectory is split into sliding windows of LLM calls. The judge sees the window rendered as a transcript (preceding events tagged [context] , and the callable event tagged with <<CALL n>> ) and LLM labels the provided event in the window in a single response. Local context lets the judge disambiguate repeated commands by surrounding state. 2. Forced tool-use output. The judge cannot reply with free-form text. Its only allowed output is a single call to the submit_classifications tool whose schema only accepts an enum . Outputs are validated client-side before acceptance. B.1.2 Classification rubric Table lists every field the judge assigns to a call. R1–R5 carry the bulk of the behavioural signal, R6 supplies a coarse-phase label used in Gantt-style trajectory plots, R7 is a reliability self-report used to flag low-confidence buckets in downstream analyses, and R8 disambiguates the raw error status, because a non-zero bash exit ( grep returning “no match”, pytest reporting test failures, etc.) is often not a tool malfunction.
